tier_reason: Doc/Manual/Python.html section 35.6.5.1 has a first-party table of per-call timings in microseconds (callme0/4/8: Default 0.15/0.26/0.32, -fastproxy 0.09/0.16/0.20, -builtin 0.07/0.14/0.17), with no harness, hardware, compiler, Python version or repeat count stated. The comparison is between SWIG's own code-generation modes, not against another binding tool, so it is tier C.

corrections.caveats: The baseline is SWIG's own default proxy-class mode, not another binding tool: the manual makes no numeric comparison against SIP, pybind11, Boost.Python, nanobind or Cython, and two WebSearches for third-party SWIG call-overhead numbers found none (nanobind's and pybind11's benchmark pages do not include SWIG). The manual itself says the overhead is 'reduced slightly' with -fastproxy. No hardware, compiler, Python version, repeat count or harness is given for the table; no benchmark script was found for it (Examples/python/performance returns 404). Trade-offs from the same manual: -fastproxy (also turned on by -O) hides docstrings, Python annotations and default argument values in the generated proxy class unless -olddefs is added, it is silently ignored for methods that use %pythonprepend or similar additions, and -builtin and -fastproxy do not work with Py_LIMITED_API. Another table in the same manual shows the -threads option slowing the profiletest.i run (single threaded 9.6 s vs fully multithreaded 15.5 s, about 60% slower). LICENSE: the SWIG tool is GPL-3.0-or-later with portions under LICENSE-UNIVERSITIES; the Lib and Examples directories (the runtime code copied into generated wrappers) are under a permissive grant ('copy, modify, distribute ... without restriction'). The lead's statement that the generated output is not covered by the GPL was not independently verified here.

notes: Numbers and the 1.6-1.7x (-fastproxy) and 1.9-2.1x (-builtin) ratios check out as derived from page data. Shortcoming to record: off-baseline (internal mode comparison only, no incumbent such as pybind11 or Cython measured), no methodology or harness for the table, and -fastproxy loses docstrings/annotations/defaults without -olddefs. Metadata confirmed: 6.3k stars, 1.3k forks, not archived, not a fork, last commit 2026-10-07 on master, GPL-3.0 plus LICENSE-UNIVERSITIES plus permissive Lib/Examples terms.

tier_reason: The README 'Modifications' list carries a one-line first-party claim, 'Speed up string passing between Java and C++ (about 5-10x faster depending on string size)', against the original Dropbox string conversion, with no benchmark, string sizes, device or version. The repo's perftest app (perftest/README.md) reports absolute nanosecond timings for the fork only, with no before/after comparison and no device named, so the claim stays tier C.

corrections.caveats: First-party one-line claim with no baseline version, string sizes, device or method. The repo has an Android perftest app (perftest/, djinni_perf_benchmark.djinni) whose README shows example output for the fork alone (argString 16/128/4096/16384: 4,622/4,893/24,407/109,606 ns average; returnString same sizes: 5,285/5,605/57,891/230,499 ns) but no run of the original Dropbox code and no device or Android/NDK version, so the 5-10x figure cannot be checked from it. Code reading: the original dropbox/djinni support-lib/jni/djinni_support.cpp converts strings with miniutf-derived handwritten UTF-8/UTF-16 code that substitutes U+FFFD for invalid sequences and unpaired surrogates; the Snapchat fork's jniStringFromUTF8/jniUTF8FromString now use std::wstring_convert with std::codecvt_utf8_utf16, which is deprecated since C++17 and removed in C++26, and which throws std::range_error on invalid input instead of substituting (a behavior change for malformed UTF-8 or lone surrogates; inferred from the standard, not tested). A search snippet of Snap's engineering post (eng.snap.com, blocked here) said a 16 KB string took more than 2 ms through the original handwritten conversion on a fairly fast device; not verified. dropbox/djinni itself makes no performance claim, so only the fork's string-passing change has evidence. The 'array<> is an order of magnitude faster than list<>' line compares two Djinni types; the perftest example output supports it (argListInt 128: 353,718 ns vs argArrayInt 128: 8,210 ns, about 43x, derived from page data), but argArrayRecord is declared as list<RecordSixInt> in djinni_perf_benchmark.djinni, so the 'ArrayRecord' rows actually measure list<>.

notes: Claim text is quoted accurately; record otherwise correct. Shortcomings to record: one-line first-party claim with no methodology or before/after numbers; string path now relies on deprecated std::wstring_convert (removed in C++26) that throws on invalid UTF instead of substituting U+FFFD as the Dropbox original did; perftest mislabels list<> rows as array. Metadata confirmed: 238 stars, 64 forks, Apache-2.0, not archived, not a GitHub fork (README says it continues dropbox/djinni), last commit 2024-10-28 (stale). The category reflection-and-codegen is not one of wave 12's four categories; the orchestrator may want to check the filing.
